blocks.en: Introduction: The Giants of the Great Century
blocks.es_reference: Introducción: Los Gigantes del Gran Siglo

blocks.en: The century that William Carey opened was filled with giants — men and women who left everything behind to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. We cannot tell all their stories, but in this unit we will meet five of them: Adoniram Judson in Burma, David Livingstone in Africa, Hudson Taylor in China, Mary Slessor in Nigeria, and Jim Elliot in the jungles of Ecuador. Some of them labored faithfully for decades; some of them died young. But every one of them shows us what the burden for the nations looks like when it truly takes hold of a human life.
blocks.es_reference: El siglo que abrió William Carey estuvo lleno de gigantes — hombres y mujeres que lo dejaron todo para llevar el evangelio hasta lo último de la tierra. No podemos contar todas sus historias, pero en esta unidad conoceremos a cinco de ellos: Adoniram Judson en Birmania, David Livingstone en África, Hudson Taylor en China, Mary Slessor en Nigeria, y Jim Elliot en las selvas del Ecuador. Algunos de ellos trabajaron fielmente por décadas; algunos de ellos murieron jóvenes. Pero cada uno de ellos nos muestra cómo es la carga por las naciones cuando verdaderamente se apodera de una vida humana.

blocks.en: I. Adoniram Judson — Burma
blocks.es_reference: I. Adoniram Judson — Birmania

blocks.en: Adoniram Judson (1788–1850) was the first American Protestant foreign missionary. In 1812 he sailed from Boston with his young bride Ann, and on the long voyage he became convinced of Baptist convictions. Unable to remain in India, the Judsons settled in Burma in 1813. There Adoniram preached for seven long years without a single convert; the first Burmese believer was not baptized until 1819. He suffered imprisonment and torture, and he buried his wife and his children on the field. Yet he pressed on, and he gave Burma a translation of the entire Bible into the Burmese language, completed in 1840 and still in use to this day. Judson teaches us patience, for as the psalmist says, "those who sow in tears shall reap in joy" (Psalm 126:5, NKJV).
blocks.es_reference: Adoniram Judson (1788–1850) fue el primer misionero protestante extranjero de Norteamérica. En 1812 zarpó de Boston con su joven esposa Ann, y en el largo viaje llegó a convencerse de las convicciones bautistas. Sin poder permanecer en la India, los Judson se establecieron en Birmania en 1813. Allí Adoniram predicó por siete largos años sin un solo converso; el primer creyente birmano no fue bautizado hasta 1819. Sufrió encarcelamiento y tortura, y sepultó a su esposa y a sus hijos en el campo. Sin embargo, siguió adelante, y dio a Birmania una traducción de toda la Biblia al idioma birmano, terminada en 1840 y todavía en uso hasta el día de hoy. Judson nos enseña paciencia, porque como dice el salmista: "Los que sembraron con lágrimas, con regocijo segarán" (Salmo 126:5, RVG).

blocks.en: II. David Livingstone — Africa
blocks.es_reference: II. David Livingstone — África

blocks.en: David Livingstone (1813–1873) was a Scottish doctor and minister — a missionary, an explorer, and a tireless enemy of the African slave trade. Sent out by the London Missionary Society, he opened the interior of southern and central Africa both to the gospel and to the conscience of the watching world. He poured out his life for the continent he loved, traveling thousands of miles through unmapped country, and at the last his servants found him dead, kneeling in prayer beside his bed. Livingstone calls the church to care for the whole person — to hate the chains that bind men's bodies as well as the sin that binds their souls.
blocks.es_reference: David Livingstone (1813–1873) fue un médico y ministro escocés — misionero, explorador, e incansable enemigo del comercio de esclavos africano. Enviado por la Sociedad Misionera de Londres, abrió el interior del sur y del centro de África tanto al evangelio como a la conciencia del mundo que lo observaba. Derramó su vida por el continente que amaba, viajando miles de millas por tierras sin mapa, y al final sus siervos lo hallaron muerto, arrodillado en oración junto a su cama. Livingstone llama a la iglesia a cuidar de la persona entera — a aborrecer las cadenas que atan los cuerpos de los hombres tanto como el pecado que ata sus almas.

blocks.en: III. J. Hudson Taylor — China
blocks.es_reference: III. J. Hudson Taylor — China

blocks.en: J. Hudson Taylor (1832–1905) was the founder of the China Inland Mission. Converted as a boy of sixteen, this young English doctor sailed for China at twenty-one. While most missions of his day stayed safely in the coastal treaty ports, Taylor was determined to reach the vast, unevangelized interior. He adopted Chinese dress, ate Chinese food, and lived among the people in a way that shocked his European colleagues — for he would remove every needless barrier between the Chinese and Christ. In 1865 he founded the China Inland Mission on what he called a faith principle: no guaranteed salaries and no denominational backing; the mission would simply ask God for the workers and the funds. Within fifty years it had more than a thousand missionaries spread across every province of China. His most quoted words have encouraged missionaries ever since: "God's work done in God's way will never lack God's supply."
blocks.es_reference: J. Hudson Taylor (1832–1905) fue el fundador de la Misión al Interior de China. Convertido siendo un muchacho de dieciséis años, este joven médico inglés zarpó hacia China a los veintiuno. Mientras la mayoría de las misiones de su día se quedaban a salvo en los puertos costeros del tratado, Taylor estaba decidido a alcanzar el vasto interior no evangelizado. Adoptó la vestimenta china, comió comida china, y vivió entre el pueblo de una manera que escandalizó a sus colegas europeos — porque quería quitar toda barrera innecesaria entre los chinos y Cristo. En 1865 fundó la Misión al Interior de China sobre lo que él llamaba un principio de fe: sin salarios garantizados y sin respaldo denominacional; la misión sencillamente pediría a Dios los obreros y los fondos. En cincuenta años tenía más de mil misioneros repartidos por cada provincia de China. Sus palabras más citadas han alentado a los misioneros desde entonces: "La obra de Dios hecha a la manera de Dios nunca carecerá de la provisión de Dios."

blocks.en: IV. Mary Slessor — Nigeria
blocks.es_reference: IV. Mary Slessor — Nigeria

blocks.en: Mary Slessor (1848–1915) was a Scottish mill girl who became one of the great missionaries to Calabar, in what is now southeastern Nigeria. Working alone among peoples that had been considered far too dangerous for any missionary to enter, she transformed the whole Okoyong region. She made peace between warring tribes. And she ended the cruel practice of killing newborn twins, who were believed to be cursed and were abandoned to die in the bush — she gathered up the abandoned babies and raised them as her own. Mary Slessor reminds us that God delights to use the lowly, and that a single fearless life, surrendered to Him, can overturn the cruelty of generations.
blocks.es_reference: Mary Slessor (1848–1915) fue una obrera de fábrica escocesa que llegó a ser una de las grandes misioneras a Calabar, en lo que hoy es el sureste de Nigeria. Trabajando sola entre pueblos que habían sido considerados demasiado peligrosos para que ningún misionero entrara, transformó toda la región de Okoyong. Hizo la paz entre tribus en guerra. Y puso fin a la cruel práctica de matar a los bebés gemelos recién nacidos, que se creía que estaban malditos y eran abandonados a morir en la maleza — ella recogía a los bebés abandonados y los criaba como suyos. Mary Slessor nos recuerda que Dios se deleita en usar a los humildes, y que una sola vida valiente, rendida a Él, puede vencer la crueldad de generaciones.

blocks.en: V. The Cost — Jim Elliot and the Martyrs
blocks.es_reference: V. El Costo — Jim Elliot y los Mártires

blocks.en: The advance of the gospel has always had a price, and across the centuries many have paid it with their lives. In 1956, five young American missionaries — Jim Elliot among them — set out to reach the Huaorani people, a tribe deep in the jungles of Ecuador who had never heard the name of Christ. As they made contact, the Huaorani attacked, and all five men were speared to death. Jim Elliot's wife, Elisabeth, was just twenty-nine years old, with a baby daughter. But the story did not end at the river's edge. In the years that followed, Elisabeth Elliot and others went back to those same people, and many of the Huaorani — including some of the very men who had killed the missionaries — were brought to faith in Christ. Years before he died, Jim Elliot had written in his journal the words that became the watchword of a generation: "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose." Their deaths were not waste, for the Lord Himself had said, "unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it produces much grain" (John 12:24, NKJV).
blocks.es_reference: El avance del evangelio siempre ha tenido un precio, y a través de los siglos muchos lo han pagado con sus vidas. En 1956, cinco jóvenes misioneros norteamericanos — Jim Elliot entre ellos — salieron a alcanzar al pueblo huaorani, una tribu en lo profundo de las selvas del Ecuador que nunca había oído el nombre de Cristo. Al hacer contacto, los huaorani atacaron, y los cinco hombres fueron atravesados con lanzas hasta morir. La esposa de Jim Elliot, Elisabeth, tenía apenas veintinueve años, con una hija pequeña. Pero la historia no terminó a la orilla del río. En los años que siguieron, Elisabeth Elliot y otros volvieron a aquel mismo pueblo, y muchos de los huaorani — incluyendo a algunos de los mismos hombres que habían matado a los misioneros — fueron llevados a la fe en Cristo. Años antes de morir, Jim Elliot había escrito en su diario las palabras que llegaron a ser el lema de una generación: "No es insensato quien da lo que no puede retener para ganar lo que no puede perder." Sus muertes no fueron en vano, porque el Señor mismo había dicho: "si el grano de trigo no cae en la tierra y muere, queda solo; mas si muere, lleva mucho fruto" (Juan 12:24, RVG).

blocks.en: Conclusion: A Pattern, Not a Relic
blocks.es_reference: Conclusión: Un Modelo, No una Reliquia

blocks.en: Judson's patience, Livingstone's compassion, Taylor's faith, Slessor's courage, and Elliot's sacrifice are not relics to be admired from a distance. They are a pattern for the present. The same Lord who called and sent these giants is calling and sending still, and the same gospel that was worth their lives is worth ours. To them and to all the faithful, the promise stands: "Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10, NKJV). Let us honor them best by finishing the work for which they died.
blocks.es_reference: La paciencia de Judson, la compasión de Livingstone, la fe de Taylor, el valor de Slessor, y el sacrificio de Elliot no son reliquias para admirar desde lejos. Son un modelo para el presente. El mismo Señor que llamó y envió a estos gigantes sigue llamando y enviando, y el mismo evangelio que valió sus vidas vale la nuestra. A ellos y a todos los fieles, la promesa permanece: "Sé fiel hasta la muerte, y yo te daré la corona de la vida" (Apocalipsis 2:10, RVG). Honrémoslos de la mejor manera, terminando la obra por la cual murieron.

sa.prompt: Tell the story of Adoniram Judson, including his patience and his gift to Burma.
sa.model: Adoniram Judson, the first American Protestant foreign missionary, sailed for Burma with his wife Ann in 1812 and preached seven long years without a single convert before the first Burmese believer was baptized in 1819. He suffered imprisonment, torture, and buried his wife and children on the field, yet he pressed on and completed a translation of the entire Bible into Burmese in 1840, still in use today — his patience shows that sowing in tears can still reap in joy.

sa.prompt: Who was David Livingstone, and what did he give his life to?
sa.model: David Livingstone was a Scottish doctor and minister who was a missionary, an explorer, and a tireless enemy of the African slave trade. Sent out by the London Missionary Society, he gave his life to opening the interior of southern and central Africa both to the gospel and to the conscience of the watching world, dying at last kneeling in prayer beside his bed.

sa.prompt: Describe Hudson Taylor's strategy and the China Inland Mission.
sa.model: While most missions of his day stayed safely in China's coastal treaty ports, Hudson Taylor's strategy was to push into the vast, unevangelized interior. He adopted Chinese dress and lived among the people to remove every needless barrier between them and Christ, and in 1865 he founded the China Inland Mission, which within fifty years had more than a thousand missionaries across every province of China.

sa.prompt: What did Hudson Taylor mean by a 'faith principle,' and what was his most famous saying?
sa.model: By a 'faith principle,' Hudson Taylor meant that the China Inland Mission would have no guaranteed salaries and no denominational backing; instead it would simply ask God for the workers and the funds needed. His most famous saying, still quoted by missionaries today, was: 'God's work done in God's way will never lack God's supply.'

sa.prompt: Tell the story of Mary Slessor and the cruelties she ended.
sa.model: Mary Slessor, a Scottish mill girl, worked alone among peoples in the Okoyong region of what is now southeastern Nigeria that had been considered too dangerous for any missionary to enter. She made peace between warring tribes and ended the cruel practice of killing newborn twins, who were believed cursed and abandoned to die in the bush; she gathered up the abandoned babies and raised them as her own.

sa.prompt: What does Mary Slessor's life teach about whom God uses?
sa.model: Mary Slessor's life teaches that God delights to use the lowly — a working-class Scottish mill girl with no formal advantages transformed an entire region through fearless, single-handed obedience. Her story shows that a single surrendered life, however humble its origins, can overturn cruelty that had gone unchallenged for generations.

sa.prompt: Tell the story of Jim Elliot and the five missionaries in Ecuador, including what happened afterward.
sa.model: In 1956, five young American missionaries, including Jim Elliot, set out to reach the Huaorani people of Ecuador, who had never heard of Christ; as they made contact, the Huaorani attacked and speared all five men to death. Jim Elliot's widow Elisabeth, only twenty-nine, later returned to those same people along with others, and many Huaorani, including some of the very men who had killed the missionaries, were brought to faith in Christ.

sa.prompt: Explain Jim Elliot's saying, 'He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.'
sa.model: Jim Elliot's saying means that giving up something temporary and perishable — like earthly life or safety — in order to gain something eternal and imperishable is not foolishness but wisdom, however it may look to the world. He was not a fool for risking his life for the Huaorani because what he gained, eternal reward and souls brought to Christ, could never be taken from him, while what he gave, his earthly life, he could never have kept forever anyway.

sa.prompt: How does the lesson use the picture of the grain of wheat (John 12:24) to explain the martyrs' deaths?
sa.model: The lesson uses John 12:24, where Jesus says a grain of wheat must fall into the ground and die in order to produce much grain, to explain that the martyrs' deaths were not waste. Just as a single seed must be buried and appear to be lost in order to multiply into a harvest, the deaths of Jim Elliot and his companions became the seed from which many Huaorani, including their former killers, were later brought to faith.

sa.prompt: Of these five lives — Judson's patience, Livingstone's compassion, Taylor's faith, Slessor's courage, Elliot's sacrifice — which speaks most to you, and why?
sa.model: This is a personal reflection question inviting the student to identify which of the five qualities — Judson's patience, Livingstone's compassion, Taylor's faith, Slessor's courage, or Elliot's sacrifice — speaks most directly to their own life and calling right now. A thoughtful answer names a specific quality and connects it honestly to a real area of the student's own walk with God.
